about: What to do about a leaked credential, per vendor, from that vendor's own documentation. Each entry carries its source and how well it was verified; the browser view shows the steps on a finding's card. Anything not confirmed in a vendor's docs is marked and worded as uncertain rather than asserted.
universal: Deleting the transcript does not undo this: the value was already sent to the model vendor as chat context, and may be in their server-side logs.
Revoke first, then issue a replacement. If downtime matters, create the replacement, move your app to it, and revoke the old one immediately after.

live_credential.headline: This credential exists on this machine and appears in AI assistant history, so treat it as known to someone else.
steps: Revoke it wherever it was issued, then create a replacement.
Update every place that used it — the copy still on disk is listed on this card.
Check the service's audit or usage log for the window between the leak and the revocation, not just that the old value is dead.

pattern.headline: This is a credential in a known vendor format found in AI assistant history.
steps: Confirm it is yours and still valid — the masked value here is enough to find it.
Revoke it at the vendor and issue a replacement.
Check the vendor's audit or usage log for the window between the leak and the revocation, not just that the old value is dead.

configuration.headline: This secret sits in plain text in an AI tool's configuration file. It is not necessarily sent to a model, but anyone who can read the file can use it.
steps: Move it out of the configuration file into your environment or a secrets manager, if the tool supports that.
If the file has been shared, synced or backed up, revoke and replace the value as well.

session_cookie.headline: A session cookie is a live sign-in. Rotating it means ending the session, not changing a key.
steps: Sign out of all sessions for that account in its security settings: that is what invalidates the cookie, and a password change on its own may not.
Change the account password as well if the service gives you no way to end sessions.
Turn on two-factor authentication, and re-enrol it or your passkeys if the session could have been used to change your security settings.

private_key.headline: A private key cannot be rotated in place: it has to be replaced everywhere it is trusted. A passphrase protects the file on disk, not a key whose plain text has been pasted into a transcript.
steps: Generate a new key pair — ssh-keygen -t ed25519, or RSA of at least 3072 bits.
Add the new public key everywhere the old one was trusted: authorized_keys files, Git hosts, cloud key lists, deploy keys and CI.
Remove the old public key from every one of those places; that removal is what actually revokes it.
Check those hosts' authentication logs for logins since the key was exposed.
Delete the exposed private key file once nothing uses it.
If it is a TLS key, have the certificate revoked by its issuer as well: until that revocation propagates, the old key still speaks for you.

connection_string.headline: A connection string carries the password and the address. Changing the password does not un-publish the host, port, database name and user.
steps: Change that database user's password: ALTER ROLE in PostgreSQL, ALTER USER … PASSWORD EXPIRE in MySQL, db.changeUserPassword in MongoDB, or Database Access in a managed console.
Disconnect sessions still using the old password — PostgreSQL leaves them running until you terminate them.
Update the connection string wherever it is configured, and avoid typing the new password where a shell history or log will keep it.
Check whether that host is reachable from the internet at all, and look through the database log for connections from addresses you do not know.

prompt.headline: A password-like string was typed into an AI assistant.
prompt.confirm_first: Decide first whether this is a real password of yours; the steps below only apply if it is.
steps: If it is a real password, change it on that service.
If the account supports it, sign out of other sessions and turn on two-factor authentication.

entropy.headline: A random-looking token near a secret-related word. Only the deep scan found it, and it may be nothing.
entropy.confirm_first: Look at the value and decide whether it is a credential of yours; the steps below only apply if it is.
steps: Look at the value and decide whether it is a credential of yours.
If it is, revoke and replace it at whichever service issued it.
On the API keys page, open the key's ⋯ menu and choose Delete API Key; it stops working at once.
Press Create Key for a replacement, and keep it in a secrets manager rather than in a file.
Use separate keys for development, test and production, so the next leak only costs you one of them.
Contact Anthropic support if you still see activity you cannot account for after replacing the key.
notes: There is no overlap window: everything using the key breaks the moment you delete it.
console.anthropic.com now redirects to platform.claude.com; both lead to the same page.
Anthropic documents no per-key request log, and recommends rotating keys every 90 days.

steps: Revoke the leaked key on the API keys page; requests using it start failing straight away.
Create a replacement scoped to a single project, with an expiry if your organisation allows one.
Update the application and confirm it works on the new key.
Check the usage page for spend between when the key leaked and when you revoked it.
notes: An sk-proj- key belongs to one project; a legacy sk- key covers the whole organisation, so replace it with a project key.
Admin keys are a separate credential that only an organisation owner can see.
OpenAI's own guide creates the replacement first — that is for planned rotation, not for a leak.

steps: For an API key, open it on the Credentials page and choose Rotate key, keeping the same restrictions; update your apps, then delete the old key.
For an OAuth client, add a second client secret, move your apps onto it, then disable and delete the old one.
For a service account key, disable it first and delete it afterwards — deletion cannot be undone.
If the service account itself is exposed, disable the account, wait at least an hour for tokens already minted from it to expire, then re-enable it.
In Logs Explorer, search that identity's API calls for service accounts, virtual machines or buckets you did not create.
notes: Deleting a service-account key does not revoke access tokens already issued from it; that is why Google's guidance is to disable the account and wait.
A deleted API key or OAuth client can be restored for 30 days; a deleted service-account key cannot.
Data Access audit logs only cover the period since you turned them on.

steps: For an API key, open it on the Credentials page, choose Rotate key, keep the same restrictions, update your apps and delete the old key.
For an OAuth client secret, add a second secret, move your apps onto it, then disable and delete the old one.
Restrict the replacement to the APIs, addresses or apps that actually need it.
notes: A deleted API key or OAuth client can be restored for 30 days.

steps: Open your Google account's Security page, go to Your devices, and sign out of the devices you do not recognise.
Change the account password if you cannot account for every session.
Check Recent security activity, and re-enrol two-step verification or your passkeys if the session could have changed those settings.
notes: A cookie is an already-signed-in session: there is nothing to re-key, so signing out is the whole of the fix.
Google documents signing out per device rather than one button that ends every session.

steps: In IAM, open the user's Security credentials tab and set the leaked key to Inactive now; that stops it working while still letting you put it back.
Create a second access key and move every application, CLI profile and CI job onto it.
Delete the inactive key once nothing is failing — a user can only hold two keys at a time.
In CloudTrail event history, look for access keys, users, roles or policies created using the leaked key.
Replace it with an IAM user or a role, never with a root-user access key.
notes: AKIA… is a long-lived user key; ASIA… is a temporary session credential that expires by itself.
The secret half is shown only when the key is created: if you have lost it, delete the key and make a new one.

AWS says it quarantines keys it finds exposed publicly with an AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policy, opens a support case and notifies you; its guidance is to leave that policy in place until you have finished cleaning up.

steps: Delete the token: classic ones under Settings → Developer settings → Tokens (classic), fine-grained ones under Fine-grained tokens.
Create a replacement — a token cannot be regenerated — and prefer a fine-grained token limited to the repositories it needs.
Update your Git credential helper, CI secrets and anything else that stored it.
Read the security log for pushes, key additions or setting changes you did not make.
For a GitHub App or OAuth app token, revoke that app's authorisation in your account settings, which kills every token it holds.
notes: GitHub revokes tokens it finds in public repositories and gists by itself.
Anyone who finds a token can revoke it through GitHub's public revocation API without owning the account; that revocation appears in your security log.
A classic token unused for a year is removed automatically.

steps: Use the token's Rotate action: GitLab issues a replacement with the same scopes and revokes the old one in one step.
Copy the new token — it is shown only once — and update whatever used the old one.
If you do not need the same scopes, revoke it instead and create a narrower token with a short expiry.
notes: Personal access tokens start with glpat-; on gitlab.com they expire within a year by default.
Audit events exist for groups and self-managed instances; the page for them on gitlab.com is not confirmed here.

steps: For a storage account key, point your apps at key2, regenerate key1, move the apps to the new key1, then regenerate key2.
Reissue every account and service SAS you signed with the regenerated key: they stop working with it.
For an application secret, add a new client secret under Certificates & secrets, deploy it, then delete the old one.
Update Azure DevOps service connections from the DevOps portal rather than editing the secret in place.
notes: A leaked storage key is both full access to the data and the power to mint SAS tokens; Microsoft suggests disallowing Shared Key access altogether.
User delegation SAS tokens are signed with Entra credentials, so regenerating account keys does not affect them.
Microsoft's advice is to keep only one of the two keys in use at a time, otherwise there is never a free key to rotate into.

steps: Open the app registration's Certificates & secrets and add a new client secret.
Deploy the new secret everywhere the app runs, then delete the old one.
Update Azure DevOps service connections from the DevOps portal rather than editing the secret in place.
notes: A secret's value is shown only once, when it is created.
The maximum lifetime is 24 months and Microsoft recommends a year or less; a certificate is the stronger option.

console.where: how to revoke a personal access token

steps: Open User settings → Personal access tokens in your organisation — dev.azure.com/{organisation}/_usersSettings/tokens — and revoke the token.
Create a replacement with the narrowest scopes and a short expiry.
Ask an administrator to check Organization settings → Audit log for PatCreated, PatRevoked and PatRegenerated events, which are kept for 90 days.
notes: Revocation is immediate and ends sessions that were using the token.
The token is 84 characters with a fixed AZDO marker near the end, which is what makes it recognisable in a transcript.
Azure DevOps revokes PATs it finds in public GitHub repositories unless the tenant has turned that off.
There is no single URL for the page: it lives under your organisation's name.

steps: Open Settings → Access Tokens, use Manage on the token, and delete or refresh it.
Create a fine-grained replacement carrying only the permissions the job needs.
Update your HF_TOKEN variables, CI secrets and the token cached by huggingface-cli login.
notes: Anyone who finds an hf_ token can invalidate it without any access to your account; Hugging Face emails the owner when that happens.
An organisation on a Team or Enterprise plan can revoke a token's access to the organisation permanently.

steps: Delete the token on the Access Tokens page of your npm account, or run npm token list and npm token delete with the token's id.
Create a granular access token limited to the packages that need it, and update your CI secrets and .npmrc.
Check your packages' version history for releases you did not publish.
notes: npm says revocation can take up to an hour to take full effect, so watch for publishes during that window.
npm token delete takes the token's id, not the token itself.

steps: Remove the token under Account settings → API tokens, then add one scoped to a single project.
Update your CI secrets and any .pypirc that held it.
Check each project's release history for versions you did not publish.
Move publishing to Trusted Publishing, so your CI no longer needs a long-lived token at all.
notes: PyPI revokes tokens it finds posted publicly and emails the owner.
Tokens start with pypi- and are shown only once.

steps: Open Account settings → Personal access tokens and deactivate the token, which is reversible, or delete it outright.
Generate a replacement with the least permission that works — read-only where that is enough — and copy it immediately.
Run docker login again wherever the old token was used, and update your CI secrets.
notes: A token's expiry cannot be changed after it is created; make a new token instead.
Docker's documentation gives no specific guidance for a leaked token, so these are its ordinary token-management steps.

steps: Open Settings & Privacy → Sign in & security → Where you're signed in, and choose Sign out of all these sessions; LinkedIn asks for your password to confirm.
Change your password as well if you cannot account for the sessions you saw there.
Turn on two-step verification if it is not on already.
notes: A li_at cookie is a signed-in session, not a key: ending the session is the only thing that invalidates it.
Signing out of all sessions ends every one except the one you are using.

steps: On the API keys page, open the key's ⋯ menu and choose Rotate key.
Pick when the old key expires: now, or after a grace period of up to seven days while you migrate.
Copy the new key — it is shown only once — and update your integration.
Watch the request logs until the old key has no traffic, then expire it.
notes: Dashboard rotation gives an overlap window, so rotating need not break production.
sk_live_ and rk_live_ are secret; pk_live_ is publishable and safe to expose.
Stripe says it monitors for exposed keys and may invalidate a leaked one itself.

steps: Invalidate the token immediately with the auth.revoke API call.
For a bot or user token, reinstall the app from OAuth & Permissions to mint a replacement.
For an app-level token, revoke and regenerate it under Basic Information → App-Level Tokens.
For an incoming webhook, delete that webhook URL in the app's settings and add a new one.
notes: xoxb- is a bot token, xoxp- a user token, xapp- an app-level token; a webhook is a secret URL, not a token.
Revoking a bot token deactivates it but does not uninstall the app.
Not confirmed in Slack's docs: whether one webhook can be revoked without affecting the others.

steps: Open Settings → API Keys and delete the exposed key; it starts returning 401 at once.
Create a replacement with the narrowest permission level that works, and copy it immediately.
Update your application configuration.
Check the email activity feed for sends you do not recognise.
notes: Keys start with "SG." and are shown only once.
SendGrid says it may delete an exposed key itself within moments of detecting it, which breaks the integration without warning.

steps: For an API key: open it and choose Delete this key, then create a replacement.
For the Auth Token, do it in stages: create a secondary token, move your integrations to it, then promote it to primary.
Check Monitor → Events for calls from addresses you do not recognise.
notes: Rotating the primary Auth Token directly breaks every integration at once; the secondary-token promotion exists to avoid that.
Each change emails the account's owners and admins.
Twilio does not document a prefix for API keys.

steps: Open Settings → Connections → Develop or manage connections and find the integration.
For an internal integration choose Refresh, which issues a new secret and invalidates the old one at once; for a personal access token, revoke it.
Update the secret everywhere it is used.
notes: New tokens start with ntn_; tokens issued before September 2024 start with secret_ and still work.
The audit log is Enterprise-only and only covers events since that plan started.

steps: Open Settings → Account → Security & Access and revoke the key; it stops working immediately.
Create a replacement and update whatever used it.
For an OAuth app, rotate the client secret, or revoke a single user token through the OAuth revoke endpoint.
notes: Admins can always manage keys; members only when an admin has enabled member API keys.
The audit log covers the last 90 days and is visible to workspace owners.

steps: For an API token, open its ⋯ menu and choose Roll: the old token stops working and the new one keeps the same permissions.
For the Global API Key, use Change in the API Keys section — but prefer replacing it with a scoped token.
Check the audit log for changes you did not make.
notes: Cloudflare recommends scoped tokens over the Global API Key, which has unscoped access to everything with no expiry.
The audit log records writes, not reads, and is available on every plan.

steps: On the Tokens page, use the token's menu to delete or regenerate it.
Copy the new secret immediately — it is shown only once — and update your integrations.
Check Settings → Security → Security History for token activity you do not recognise.
notes: A token's scope cannot be changed after creation; only renamed, regenerated or deleted.
Spaces access keys are a separate credential, rotated separately.
DigitalOcean revokes tokens it finds exposed in public GitHub repositories.

steps: Open the account tokens page, find the token and revoke it; revocation is immediate.
Create a replacement with the narrowest scope that works and an expiry, and copy it immediately.
Update your CI or local configuration.
notes: Tokens are shown only once, and project-scoped tokens cannot create new tokens.
Vercel revokes tokens it finds in public repositories, gists or npm packages.
The audit log is an Enterprise feature.

steps: On the API tokens page, revoke the token (or revoke all of them if you are unsure which leaked).
Create a replacement with an expiry, and scopes if you use scoped tokens; copy it immediately.
Update every integration that used it — revoking breaks all of them at once.
notes: A classic token carries the full access of the account that created it.
Atlassian revokes tokens it finds in public repositories.
Bitbucket's documentation mentions revocation taking up to ten minutes to propagate; whether that applies to every Atlassian token is not confirmed.

steps: Open the chat with @BotFather and send /mybots, or send /token.
Pick the bot and revoke the current token; BotFather issues a new one and the old one stops working at once.
Update the token wherever your bot runs.
notes: There is no web console and no request log for the Bot API: the token is the whole of the bot's security.
Only one token is active per bot at a time.

steps: Open your application → Bot and press Reset Token, confirming with two-factor authentication if you have it on.
Copy the new token immediately and restart your bot with it.
For a webhook, delete it in Server Settings → Integrations → Webhooks and create a new one.
notes: Resetting invalidates the old token at once, with no grace period: running bots disconnect immediately.
Discord scans public GitHub content and invalidates leaked tokens itself.
The server audit log records webhook changes for 45 days; token resets are not logged there.
